# `ts/switch-exhaustiveness-check`

**A `switch` on a union handles every member**

| | |
|---|---|
| **Pack** | `@codelaw/rules-ts` (npm) |
| **Languages** | TypeScript, TSX |
| **Turned on by** | `codelaw:ts/type-checked` at `error` |
| **Severity when named without one** | `error` |
| **Options** | none — severity only |
| **Fix** | `manual` — no automatic fix; the steps are under *How to fix* (what each missing member should do is the author's decision) |
| **Stability** | `preview` — runs only with `preview = true` |
| **Since** | 0.4.4 |
| **Tags** | `types` |
| **Ported from** | `typescript-eslint/switch-exhaustiveness-check` |

## What it checks

A `switch` whose value is a union of literal types (string, number or boolean literals, enum
members, `null`, `undefined`) has a `case` for every member, or a `default`.

**Why:** When a member is added to the union, a `switch` that silently skips it lets the new value
fall through to whatever comes after; with every member handled, TypeScript points at each `switch`
that needs the new case.

## Configuration

Everything below goes in `codelaw.toml` at the repo root. The same keys work as `[tool.codelaw]` in `pyproject.toml` or `"codelaw"` in `package.json` ([SR-CONFIG](../../../records/0110_config.md)).

### Turn it on

**Install the pack** (`codelaw init` does it for the languages it finds):

```bash
npm install --save-dev @codelaw/rules-ts
```

**Then extend a preset that turns it on** — `codelaw:ts/type-checked` sets it to `error`:

```toml
preview = true                        # pack rules are preview today
extends = ["codelaw:ts/type-checked"]
```

- **A rule exists only once its pack is loaded** through `extends`; naming it in `[rules]` without that is an unknown rule id (exit 2).
- **Without `preview = true`** the rule is skipped and codelaw warns that it is preview.

### Severity

```toml
[rules]
"ts/switch-exhaustiveness-check" = "warn"    # error | warn | info | off
```

- **`error`** fails the run (exit 1) · **`warn`** fails only with `--max-warnings N` · **`info`** never fails · **`off`** turns it off.
- **Naming it with a severity turns it on** even when no preset does.

### For a group of files

A `[scope.<name>]` gives some files their own setting, applied after `[rules]` — the `tests` scope `codelaw:js/recommended` ships (`**/*.test.*`, `**/*.spec.*`); naming it extends it, so its files stay:

```toml
[scope.tests]
rules = { "ts/switch-exhaustiveness-check" = "off" }
```

A scope's `remap` changes whole severities in its files, after everything else: `remap = { error = "warn" }` never fails the run there.

### Warn locally, fail in CI

The `ci` profile runs when `CI` is set; `local` otherwise; `--profile <name>` or `CODELAW_PROFILE` picks one.

```toml
[profile.local.rules]
"ts/switch-exhaustiveness-check" = "warn"

[profile.ci.rules]
"ts/switch-exhaustiveness-check" = "error"
```

### In `pyproject.toml` or `package.json`

```toml
# pyproject.toml
[tool.codelaw.rules]
"ts/switch-exhaustiveness-check" = { severity = "warn" }
```

```json
{
  "codelaw": {
    "rules": {
      "ts/switch-exhaustiveness-check": {"severity": "warn"}
    }
  }
}
```

### Silence one finding

An inline `codelaw-ignore` always needs a reason; `expires=`, `warn_days=` and `by=` date it ([SR-LINTER](../../../records/0106_linter.md) decision 6).

- **TypeScript:** `// codelaw-ignore ts/switch-exhaustiveness-check: <reason>`
- **Dated:** `// codelaw-ignore ts/switch-exhaustiveness-check expires=2026-12-31 by=you@example.com: <reason>`

### Keep today's findings, fail on new ones

```bash
codelaw baseline add --rule ts/switch-exhaustiveness-check --expires 2026-12-31 --reason "<why>"
```

See [SR-BASELINE](../../../records/0104_baseline-and-deprecations.md).

### See what applies

```bash
codelaw explain ts/switch-exhaustiveness-check       # what it wants, why, how to fix
codelaw check --rule ts/switch-exhaustiveness-check  # only this rule
codelaw config --print --for <file>                  # the resolved setting, and where it came from
```

## How to fix

1. Add a `case` for each member of the value's type the `switch` leaves out (hover the value, or
   read its type, to list them).
2. If the members left out really share one behaviour, add a `default` instead.

## Examples

### TypeScript

#### Don't

```ts
type Shape = "circle" | "square";
export function sides(s: Shape): number {
  switch (s) {
    case "circle":
      return 0;
  }
  return -1;
}
```

#### Do

```ts
type Shape = "circle" | "square";
export function sides(s: Shape): number {
  switch (s) {
    case "circle":
      return 0;
    case "square":
      return 4;
  }
}
```

### TSX

#### Don't

```tsx
type Shape = "circle" | "square";
export function sides(s: Shape): number {
  switch (s) {
    case "circle":
      return 0;
  }
  return -1;
}
```

#### Do

```tsx
type Shape = "circle" | "square";
export function sides(s: Shape): number {
  switch (s) {
    case "circle":
      return 0;
    default:
      return 4;
  }
}
```

## Differences from the source

A `switch` with a `default` is never reported (typescript-eslint's
`considerDefaultExhaustiveForUnions` set to `true`), and none of the rule's options are offered: a
value whose type is not made only of literal types (`string`, an object union) is not checked
(`requireDefaultForNonUnion`), and a `default` in an exhaustive `switch` is allowed
(`allowDefaultCaseForExhaustiveSwitch`). typescript-eslint's suggestion that writes the missing cases
is not offered: SR-TYPES's questions answer whether members are missing, not which.
